descriptionVi: Bài đọc ngắn về thói quen hằng ngày của một sinh viên.
descriptionEn: A short text about a university student's daily routine.
paragraphs: Lan is a university student in Da Nang. She gets up at six o'clock every morning and runs along the beach for thirty minutes. After that, she takes a shower and has breakfast with her parents. Usually she eats bread with eggs and drinks a cup of tea. She likes this quiet time before the busy day begins, and she often talks with her father about the news.

Her first class starts at eight. She goes to school by bike because it is cheap and good for her health. In the afternoon, she studies English in the library with her friend Hoa. They practise speaking and read short stories together.

Lan goes home at five. She helps her mother cook dinner, and the family eats together at seven. In the evening, she watches one episode of her favourite series, then goes to bed at ten thirty. On Sundays she does not have classes, so she visits her grandmother.

paragraphs: Hanoi is famous for its street food. Every morning, thousands of people sit on small plastic stools beside the road and eat a hot bowl of pho. A bowl usually costs between forty and sixty thousand dong, so it is cheap for both local people and tourists.

Another popular dish is bun cha. It is grilled pork served with cold rice noodles, fresh herbs and a sweet, sour sauce. Many visitors say it tastes best at lunchtime, when the meat is fresh from the grill. Egg coffee is a special drink in Hanoi. It is made with egg yolk, sugar and strong coffee, and it tastes a little like dessert.

If you want to eat street food safely, choose a busy stall. A lot of customers means that the food is fresh. Also look for clean bowls and ask for less ice in your drink. Finally, bring some small notes, because many sellers cannot change large money.

On the first day, we swam and built sand castles. The water was warm and the beach was clean. On Saturday we took a cable car to Ba Na Hills. descriptionVi: Vì sao thức khuya học bài lại phản tác dụng.
descriptionEn: Why staying up late to study often backfires.
paragraphs: Many students believe that staying up late to study is the best way to prepare for an exam. However, research on sleep suggests the opposite. During sleep, the brain organises the information we learned during the day and stores it in long-term memory. When we do not sleep enough, this process is interrupted, and we forget much more.

One well-known experiment compared two groups of students who learned the same list of words. The first group slept for eight hours after studying, while the second group stayed awake all night. Two days later, the students who had slept remembered about forty percent more words. Interestingly, the effect was still visible a week later.

Sleep also affects concentration and mood. Teenagers need between eight and ten hours of sleep each night, but surveys show that most get fewer than seven. Using a phone before bed makes the problem worse, because the bright light tells the brain that it is still daytime.

Experts therefore recommend a few simple habits: go to bed at the same time every day, stop using screens an hour before sleeping, and avoid heavy meals late in the evening. Students who follow this advice often find that they can study for a shorter time but achieve better results.

descriptionVi: Cách nhận biết đánh giá giả khi mua hàng online.
descriptionEn: How to spot fake reviews when you shop online.
paragraphs: Online shopping has changed the way people buy everything from shoes to sofas. Instead of asking a shop assistant for advice, customers now read reviews written by strangers. A recent survey found that nine out of ten shoppers check at least one review before they buy a product, and many say they trust these reviews almost as much as recommendations from friends.

Unfortunately, not every review is honest. Some companies pay people to write fake five-star comments, while others post negative reviews about their competitors. Researchers estimate that up to one in five reviews on some websites may be false.

There are several signs that a review might be fake. It may use extremely emotional language, repeat the product name many times, or contain no specific details about how the product was used. Real reviews usually mention both good and bad points, and they often include photos taken by the customer.

To protect yourself, read reviews from several websites rather than only one, pay attention to the three-star reviews because they tend to be more balanced, and check whether the reviewer has bought other products. Being a careful reader can save you both money and disappointment.

titleVi: Viết email công việc hiệu quả
descriptionVi: Các nguyên tắc viết email rõ ràng, ngắn gọn và chuyên nghiệp.
descriptionEn: Principles for writing clear, short and professional emails.
paragraphs: Most office workers spend more than two hours a day reading and writing emails, yet many of these messages are unclear or too long. A well-written email saves time for both the sender and the reader, and it also creates a professional impression.

The subject line is the first thing the reader sees. It should describe the purpose in a few words, for example 'Meeting request: project budget, Tuesday' rather than 'Hello' or 'Important'. In the opening sentence, state clearly why you are writing. If you need an answer, explain what you need and give a deadline.

Keep paragraphs short and use simple words. A long, complicated sentence may look impressive, but it makes the reader work harder. If you have several questions, use a numbered list so that the reader can reply point by point. Avoid capital letters for whole sentences, since they can look like shouting.

Finally, read your message before sending it. Check the names, the dates and any attached files. A common mistake is writing 'see the attachment' and forgetting to attach it. Ending with a polite phrase such as 'Kind regards' is enough; you do not need to write more than one closing sentence.

titleEn: How to Keep Your Passwords Safe
descriptionVi: Mật khẩu mạnh, trình quản lý mật khẩu và xác thực hai yếu tố.
descriptionEn: Strong passwords, password managers and two-factor authentication.
paragraphs: Every year, millions of online accounts are stolen, and in most cases the reason is a weak password. Security experts say that the most common passwords in the world are still '123456' and 'password'. Hackers do not need clever tools to break these; a simple program can test thousands of guesses every second.

A strong password should be long rather than complicated. Passwords with at least twelve characters are much harder to guess. One popular method is to combine four unrelated words, such as 'purple-bridge-coffee-lamp'. This is easy for a person to remember but very difficult for a computer to crack.

Another important rule is never to use the same password for different accounts. If a hacker steals your password from a small shopping site, he or she will immediately try it on your email and bank accounts. To manage many different passwords, experts recommend a password manager, which stores them safely and fills them in automatically.

Finally, turn on two-factor authentication whenever it is available. With this system, you need both your password and a second proof of identity, usually a code sent to your phone. Even if a hacker learns your password, he or she cannot enter your account without the code.

Before eating, the youngest children invite the older people to start the meal. This is a way to show respect. The older people often put the best pieces of food into the children's bowls.

During dinner, family members talk about their day. Children tell stories about school, and parents share news from work. Phones are usually put away. After the meal, the children help to clean the table and wash the dishes. Many people say that these small daily moments make a family close.

descriptionEn: A passage with True/False/Not Given questions.
paragraphs: Bicycle-sharing schemes first appeared in Amsterdam in 1965, when a group of activists painted fifty bicycles white and left them unlocked in the streets for anyone to use. The experiment failed within days because most of the bicycles were stolen or thrown into the canals. Nevertheless, the idea did not disappear.

The first modern system opened in Copenhagen in 1995. Users paid a small coin deposit to unlock a bike, similar to a shopping trolley. Later systems used smart cards and mobile phones, which allowed the operators to track every bicycle and charge users according to the time they rode.

Today, more than 1,600 cities around the world offer some kind of bike-sharing service, and the largest schemes, in China, have hundreds of thousands of bicycles. Supporters argue that the schemes reduce traffic jams and air pollution and encourage people to exercise. Critics point out that in some cities, thousands of unused bikes have been abandoned on pavements, causing new problems.

A study in London found that most users were not former car drivers but people who had previously travelled by bus or on foot. This suggests that bike-sharing does not always reduce car use as much as governments hope. However, many cities are still expanding their schemes because they are cheap to build compared with new metro lines.

titleVi: Nghịch lý của sự lựa chọn
descriptionVi: Vì sao quá nhiều lựa chọn có thể khiến người tiêu dùng do dự và kém hài lòng.
descriptionEn: Why too many options can leave consumers hesitant and less satisfied.
paragraphs: In 2000, two psychologists, Sheena Iyengar and Mark Lepper, set up a tasting table in an upmarket supermarket in California. On some days the table displayed twenty-four varieties of jam; on others, only six. The larger display attracted more attention, with sixty percent of passers-by stopping to taste. Yet only three percent of those who saw the large display made a purchase, compared with thirty percent of those who saw the small one.

This finding, which became known as the 'paradox of choice', challenged the assumption that more options always benefit consumers. Barry Schwartz, who popularised the concept, argued that an abundance of alternatives can lead to what he termed decision paralysis. When faced with too many possibilities, people find it hard to compare them, fear making the wrong selection, and sometimes abandon the decision altogether.

Even when a choice is made, satisfaction may suffer. Schwartz distinguished between 'maximisers', who search exhaustively for the best possible option, and 'satisficers', who accept an option that is good enough. Maximisers frequently achieve objectively better outcomes, such as higher salaries, but they report lower happiness, partly because they are haunted by the thought that a superior alternative was overlooked.

Subsequent research has qualified these claims. A meta-analysis of nearly fifty experiments concluded that the negative effect of large assortments is not universal; it appears mainly when the options are difficult to compare, when the decision-maker lacks clear preferences, or when no single option stands out. Where people already know what they want, additional choices can be beneficial rather than burdensome.

For designers of websites and services, the practical lesson is not simply to offer fewer products, but to help users navigate. Filters, sensible default options and clear recommendations can preserve the benefits of variety while reducing the mental effort required to choose.

titleVi: Đô thị hoá và đa dạng sinh học
descriptionVi: Thành phố có thực sự gây hại cho thiên nhiên hay có thể là môi trường sống mới?
descriptionEn: Are cities really harmful to nature, or can they be new habitats?
paragraphs: More than half of the world's population now lives in cities, and the United Nations projects that this share will reach nearly seventy percent by 2050. Since cities cover only about three percent of the Earth's land surface, urbanisation is often presented as an environmental success story: concentrated populations, it is argued, leave more space for wilderness.

However, the ecological footprint of a city extends far beyond its boundaries. Urban residents depend on distant farms for food, on remote reservoirs for water and on power stations, sometimes hundreds of kilometres away, for energy. Moreover, the expansion of cities frequently occurs on fertile land, forcing agriculture onto marginal areas, including forests and wetlands.

Within cities themselves, biodiversity has long been assumed to be poor. Recent studies have complicated this picture. Some European capitals contain more plant species than the surrounding countryside, partly because gardeners import exotic varieties, and partly because a patchwork of parks, cemeteries and railway embankments offers a wide range of habitats. Peregrine falcons, which nest on cliffs in nature, have adapted to skyscrapers, where pigeons provide an abundant food supply.

Nevertheless, this diversity is unevenly distributed and often dominated by generalist species that thrive alongside humans, such as foxes, rats and crows. Specialist species with narrow requirements decline as green space is fragmented. Ecologists therefore emphasise connectivity: green corridors that link isolated parks allow animals to move, feed and breed.

The challenge for planners, then, is not to choose between dense cities and nature, but to design density that accommodates nature. Measures such as green roofs, wildlife-friendly street lighting and protected river banks have already produced measurable gains in cities as different as Singapore and Berlin.

titleVi: Chuẩn bị cho buổi phỏng vấn xin việc
descriptionVi: Nghiên cứu công ty, phương pháp STAR và cách đặt câu hỏi ngược lại.
descriptionEn: Researching the company, the STAR method and asking your own questions.
paragraphs: A job interview is not simply a test of your qualifications; it is also an opportunity for the employer to judge whether you will fit into the team. Candidates who prepare thoroughly tend to appear more confident, and confidence is often interpreted as competence.

Preparation begins with research. Read the company's website, recent news and the job description carefully. Try to identify the two or three skills that the employer values most, and prepare a specific example for each. Recruiters generally prefer concrete stories to general claims: instead of saying 'I am a good leader', describe a project where you organised a team and achieved a measurable result.

Many interviewers use behavioural questions such as 'Tell me about a time you disagreed with a colleague'. A useful structure for answering is known as STAR: describe the Situation, explain the Task you were responsible for, outline the Action you took and, finally, state the Result. This prevents rambling answers and demonstrates logical thinking.

Candidates should also prepare questions of their own. Asking about training opportunities or the team's biggest challenge shows genuine interest, whereas asking only about salary and holidays may give the impression that you are more interested in benefits than in the work. Finally, send a short thank-you email within twenty-four hours. It is a small gesture, but it keeps your name in the interviewer's mind.
